subject: ophthalmology
title: Diseases of the orbit

steps.tx: The cardinal sign of space-occupying orbital pathology is **proptosis**, defined as forward displacement of the globe beyond the orbital rim, measured with a Hertel exophthalmometer. Axial proptosis implies an intraconal lesion within the rectus muscle cone, such as an optic nerve glioma, meningioma or cavernous hemangioma. Non-axial proptosis displaces the globe away from an extraconal mass: superotemporal lacrimal gland tumors push the globe downward and inward, whereas ethmoid mucoceles displace it laterally. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging delineate bony architecture and soft-tissue margins.
steps.say: Proptosis describes the abnormal forward protrusion of the eyeball from the orbit, most accurately quantified using a Hertel exophthalmometer. When the globe is pushed directly straight forward along its visual axis, the pathology lies within the intraconal space, such as an optic nerve sheath meningioma or cavernous hemangioma. Non axial proptosis occurs when an extraconal lesion pushes the eye off center; for example, a lacrimal gland neoplasm pushes the eyeball downward and inward. High resolution computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging map the lesion precisely.

vis.caption: Axial proptosis (intraconal mass) vs eccentric proptosis (extraconal orbital mass).

steps.tx: The commonest cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults is **thyroid eye disease**, an autoimmune inflammation driven by autoantibodies against thyroid-stimulating hormone receptors shared by thyroid cells and orbital fibroblasts. Activated fibroblasts secrete glycosaminoglycans, producing marked extraocular muscle belly enlargement that spares tendons, alongside retrobulbar adipogenesis. Key signs include eyelid retraction, lid lag, chemosis, and restrictive strabismus tethering the inferior and medial recti. Apical muscle crowding compresses the optic nerve, producing compressive optic neuropathy that demands urgent intravenous methylprednisolone pulses or surgical orbital decompression.
steps.say: Thyroid eye disease is the leading cause of proptosis in adults, driven by an autoimmune process targeting orbital fibroblasts and extraocular muscles. Stimulated fibroblasts produce hydrophilic mucopolysaccharides, causing massive muscle swelling with tendon sparing and increased orbital fat volume. Patients present with upper eyelid retraction, stare, restrictive double vision and proptosis, usually involving the inferior and medial rectus muscles. In severe cases, swollen muscles at the orbital apex can compress the optic nerve, causing visual drop that demands prompt high dose intravenous steroid therapy or surgical decompression.

vis.alt: Composite image of a patient with proptosis and lid retraction, next to a coronal CT scan showing enlarged inferior and medial rectus muscles, characteristic of Thyroid Eye Disease.
vis.caption: Thyroid eye disease: clinical signs and characteristic muscle enlargement on CT

steps.tx: A pediatric emergency, acute **orbital cellulitis** most commonly arises from contiguous bacterial spread across the thin lamina papyracea from adjacent ethmoid sinusitis. Patients present with fever, periorbital edema, proptosis, chemosis, and painful ophthalmoplegia. These cardinal signs distinguish post-septal orbital cellulitis from pre-septal cellulitis, where ocular motility, pupillary reflexes and globe position remain normal. Management mandates urgent admission, contrast-enhanced computed tomography to detect subperiosteal abscesses, and intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes, with surgical drainage indicated for non-resolving abscess collections.
steps.say: Orbital cellulitis is a dangerous bacterial infection that usually spreads into the orbit from ethmoid sinusitis across the thin lamina papyracea. The patient presents with high fever, swollen eyelids, significant proptosis, conjunctival chemosis and painful limitation of eye movements. These orbital signs are critical because they separate true post septal infection from milder preseptal cellulitis, where vision, ocular movement and pupil responses stay entirely normal. Treatment requires urgent hospital admission for intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and contrast computed tomography to identify any subperiosteal abscess requiring drainage.

vis.alt: Sagittal and axial orbital views comparing preseptal cellulitis anterior to the orbital septum with postseptal orbital cellulitis and subperiosteal abscess from ethmoid sinusitis.
vis.caption: Preseptal cellulitis vs postseptal orbital cellulitis and subperiosteal abscess.

steps.tx: Orbital venous drainage communicates directly with intracranial venous sinuses, predisposing to septic **cavernous sinus thrombosis**. Septic emboli spread via ophthalmic veins, rapidly causing bilateral proptosis, chemosis, eyelid edema, and complete ophthalmoplegia from third, fourth and sixth cranial nerve involvement, with ophthalmic division sensory loss. Carotid-cavernous fistulas represent an alternative vascular emergency, where high-pressure arterial flow causes pulsatile proptosis, a loud orbital bruit abolished by carotid compression, and tortuous corkscrew episcleral vessels, diagnosed by magnetic resonance angiography and treated by endovascular embolization.
steps.say: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a life threatening complication of facial or orbital infections that spread through the valveless ophthalmic veins. Infection causes thrombotic occlusion within the cavernous sinus, leading to rapid development of bilateral proptosis, marked chemosis and paralysis of the third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves. Patients are toxic with high swinging fever and severe headache. Another important vascular condition is a carotid cavernous fistula, which produces pulsatile proptosis, engorged corkscrew episcleral vessels and an audible orbital bruit. Neuroimaging and interventional embolization provide definitive management.
